**The rule.** Before quoting a rectangle as a measurement of a term, ask which
pixels in it the term can reach. If the answer is "not all of them", the number
is a mixture and the mixture ratio is a property of the pose, not of the term.
And a negative control must remove ONE term: an arm that deletes a whole
subsystem measures the subsystem. Where an existing flag is the only arm
available, add the narrow one before publishing -- it is a page param and a
multiply by zero, and here it changed a 77.5 per cent headline into a 44.5 per
cent one on a rectangle that could actually carry it (44.5 is the verifier's
HEAD re-measurement; 51.6 was a mid-lane reading, corrected 2026-08-20, see
rendering.md 2.12.2).

### A SHOT CAN BE IN THE MANIFEST AND IN NO POSE BRANCH, AND THEN IT PHOTOGRAPHS THE SPAWN WITH EVERY FIELD READING CORRECT

Found by RN-2169, 2026-08-20, while committing a pose a verifier had asked for.

`artframe.js` holds two things: a `SHOTS` table of manifest rows (site, yaw, pitch, sun, rectangles) and, separately, a flat chain of `if (name === 'forestfloor' || name === 'midfield') { ... }` blocks that actually TELEPORT and AIM. The chain has **no final else**. A shot added to the table and not to the chain is therefore never posed: the probe photographs wherever `--scenario=walk` spawned the capsule, and `valid` is true, the committed rectangles are measured, the sun solve converges, the render stats are real, and the report is entirely correct about the wrong place on the planet.

The new shot did exactly this on its first run. What gave it away was not a check: it was `setup: {}` where the site's own branch would have published `eyeAltM`, and `vramMB` 82.4 where that site reads 104.2. Both are noticeable only to someone who already knows the answer, which means **the defect is invisible to a new shot, which is the only kind of shot that can have it**.

This is `Controller.teleport` discarding its altitude argument (RN-2065) one layer up, and it has the same shape: an API that silently ignores an input keeps a whole class of measurement from ever being attempted, because the attempt appears to work. It is also why the two-table split is dangerous: a manifest row LOOKS like the complete declaration of a shot and is only half of one.

**The rule.** When a feature is declared in a data table and enacted by a separate dispatch, the dispatch needs a final else that REFUSES, or the two need to be one structure. Until then, the first thing to check on any new row is that its setup block ran, not that its output looks plausible. Adding a row without adding it to the dispatch is now called out in a comment on the dispatch line itself.

### A 4 MB REPORT TRUNCATED THROUGH A PIPE REPORTS AS "THE PROBE RETURNED NOTHING"

Found by RN-2169, 2026-08-20, on the same run.

`writeshot.mjs` reads all of stdin and `JSON.parse`s it in one go, which is correct. On this box, piping a **4.3 MB** report from `run.mjs` into it through Git Bash truncates the stream, and the error printed is `writeshot: stdin was not the JSON report`. That message is indistinguishable from the real failure it was written for, a probe that returned nothing or threw, and the same command had worked all evening on 2.0 to 3.4 MB reports from other shots. The variable is the size of the base64 `png` field, which is a property of how much detail is in the frame.

The lane initially read it as a probe bug and went looking in the probe. Redirecting `run.mjs` to a FILE and feeding `writeshot` from the file succeeds every time on the identical report.

**The rule.** Do not pipe a multi-megabyte report between processes on this box: write it to a file in your own scratch directory and read the file. And when a harness message describes a *content* failure ("not the JSON report"), rule out *transport* before believing it, because a truncated stream and an empty one produce the same sentence.

### A CONTROL THAT ERRORS ON ONE POSE AND RETURNS A BYTE-IDENTICAL NULL ON ANOTHER IS NOT A CONTROL, AND THE NULL IS THE DANGEROUS HALF

Found by RN-2287 (World Audit R2), 2026-08-21, on a flag that has been in
`PAGE_PARAMS` since RN-1954.

The aerial frames carry a hard, regular, texel-toothed dark region across the
mid-field, which R1 attributed to the last shadow cascade. `?shadowcast=0` is
the shipped isolator for exactly that term, and RN-1954 documents it in one
line: "the light simply stops writing and sampling a depth map". Run at
`flyovernoon`, one flag apart, fresh process, it moved **every published
rectangle by zero counts** and left the region visually untouched. Read at face
value that is a refutation: the region is not the cascade.

**It is not a refutation, because the same flag run at `machine` drives the
build into `GL_INVALID_OPERATION: glDrawElements: Mismatch between texture
format and sampler type (signed/unsigned/float/shadow)` x256**, which
`run.mjs` correctly fails the probe on. A flag cannot both be a clean no-op on
one pose and a GL error storm on another and still be doing what its
documentation says. So the null at `flyovernoon` is uninterpretable: it is
equally consistent with "the term does not paint this region", "the flag never
reached the terrain path", and "the sampler is erroring and the driver is
returning a constant".

Two things generalise, and the second is the one worth carrying.

1. **Run a control's ARMING PROOF on a pose where the term is unmistakable
   before you read its result on the pose you care about.** Here that cost one
   run and it converted a confident wrong finding into a correct open question.
   The catalogue already says a control whose arming step silently fails is
   indistinguishable from a passing control; this is the same shape where the
   arming step fails **loudly on a different pose than the one you ran**.
2. **A byte-identical null across every rectangle is a stronger signal of an
   inert instrument than of an inert term.** A real term that genuinely does
   not reach a rectangle still usually moves something by settle-tick jitter.
   Zero counts on five rectangles at once is the signature this file already
   records under "a metric that is flat in its own independent variable".

The audit's own honest statement, kept because it is the model: the region
survives `?shadowcast=0`, `?clouds=0`, `?splat=0` and `?canopy=0`, so its cause
is **undiagnosed**, and the shadow lane's first deliverable is an isolator that
works rather than a fix.

### A VALUE DERIVED FROM AN OBJECT THAT STOPS BEING UPDATED READS AS THIS FRAME'S ANSWER

Found by RN-2289 (World Audit R2), 2026-08-21, by adding the first night frame
this project has ever taken.

`Systems.ts` computes `lit = sky.elevation(observer.up) > -0.03` and hands
`on = false` to `ShadowRig.update` below the horizon. That function's loop does
`if (!this.active) continue` **before** it writes `light.position` and
`light.target.position`. `Frame.publishSun` then derives the post stack's
world-space sun direction from exactly those two positions -- deliberately,
"derived rather than stored, so it cannot go stale", which is the right instinct
applied to the wrong pair of objects: the derivation cannot go stale, and the
things it derives from can.

So at any sub-horizon sun, `post.sunWorld` is **the last daylight sun**.
Measured at the new `meadownight` pose: the probe's `upCheck` (the difference
between a lat/lon reconstruction of `dot(up, sunDir)` and the engine's own
`sky.elevationDot`) reads **0.508**, where every other shot in the file reads
0.000, and the derived `sunElevDeg` reads **+14.83 degrees** for a sun the same
report pins at dot **-0.251**. The two are near-exact negatives, which is what
made it findable.

Two consumers are affected and neither errors. `ContactPass` marches along that
vector and its only guard is `sunWorld.lengthSq() < 0.25`, which a stale UNIT
vector passes with room to spare, so contact shadows are still being marched at
night along yesterday's bearing. And any probe that reads
`__ofPost.state().sun` -- `artframe.js`'s whole sun-bearing block does --
publishes a mirrored azimuth with every other field reading correct.

**The rule.** When a value is derived from mutable state, ask what happens to
the derivation when the state stops being written, not only when it is written
wrongly. A derived value inherits its freshness from its inputs and reports
nothing about it. The cheap fix in this shape is either to publish the source
directly (the sky already owns `sunDirection`) or to publish a validity flag
beside the derived value, and `upCheck` reading 0.000 on twenty-four poses and
0.508 on the twenty-fifth is the argument for the second: **an invariant that
holds everywhere except in the one regime nobody photographs is worth
publishing precisely so that the day somebody photographs it, it says so.**

**FIXED 2026-08-21 by RN-2307**, in `ShadowRig.update`: the off path now writes
`light.target.position = eye` and `light.position = eye + sunDir * BACKOFF`
before the `continue`, so the pair `publishSun` derives from is this frame's
sun at every hour. `meadownight` `upCheck` **0.508 -> 0.000** and `sunElevDeg`
**+14.83 -> -14.57 degrees** against an `elevDot` of -0.251 (asin(-0.251) =
-14.54). No ortho fit, no texel snap and no `publishCascade` run on that path,
so the skipped draw calls stay skipped.

### `vite preview` SNAPSHOTS `dist` AT STARTUP, SO A REBUILD UNDER A RUNNING PREVIEW SERVES THE OLD PAGE, AND THE SENTINEL YOU CHECKED AT BOOT KEEPS PASSING (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2305)

`vite preview` serves `dist` through `sirv` in its non-dev mode, which builds
its file map **once, at startup**. Rebuild under a running preview and the
server keeps serving the page it read when it started: the old `index.html`,
naming the old hashed bundle, which it still holds even though that file is no
longer on disk. Nothing errors. The page loads, the probe passes, every field
in the report is correctly formatted, and the frame is of the previous build.

This lane hit it while painting a shader intermediate to `gl_FragColor` to find
out which term drew a defect. The diagnostic build was on disk and in `dist`,
`grep` found the new expression inside `dist/assets/index-*.js`, and the
captured frame was the SHIPPED frame to the eye. The only thing that gave it
away was a hash comparison nobody had thought to make:

```
served: curl -s http://127.0.0.1:<port>/ | grep -o 'index-[A-Za-z0-9_-]*\.js'
disk:   ls web/dist/assets/index-*.js
```

They did not match, and the served name was not on disk at all.

**The sentinel does not catch this on its own.** A sentinel written into `dist`
*before* the server starts is in the startup snapshot forever, so it keeps
answering with the right bytes across any number of rebuilds. It proves *whose*
dist the server read; it does not prove *when*.

**The rule.** A served build is only the build you just made if the server was
started after it. Restart the preview on every rebuild, and make the freshness
check the **served-vs-disk bundle hash**, not the sentinel: the sentinel proves
provenance, the hash proves recency, and a measurement needs both. The
mechanical form this lane settled on is one script that kills its own preview by
a PID it wrote down, builds, re-plants the sentinel, restarts, and then prints
`sentinel`, `servedJs`, `diskJs` and `match=True/False` on one line before any
probe runs. It has a second use: after reverting a temporary diagnostic, the
bundle hash returning to the pre-diagnostic value is a byte-level proof that the
revert was complete.

### A DEAD SERVER FREES ITS PORT FOR ANOTHER LANE'S SERVER, SO A SENTINEL CHECKED ONCE IS A SENTINEL CHECKED FOR ONE MOMENT (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2305)

The loopback-shadowing entry above ("A LOOPBACK BIND SILENTLY SHADOWS A WILDCARD
BIND ON THE SAME PORT") is about two servers alive at once. This is the same
class one step later in time: **one server dies and another lane's server takes
the freed port**, and every probe after that moment measures a different
worktree's build with no error anywhere.

This lane started a preview in a backgrounded shell, sentinel-verified it
(correct bytes, correct `Get-NetTCPConnection` PID) and ran arms against it. The
backgrounded launcher then reported `exit 127` and the server died with it. A
concurrent lane's `vite preview --strictPort` -- which had been failing to bind
until then -- took the port on its next attempt, and the arms kept passing.
`Get-CimInstance Win32_Process` on the new owner named the other lane's
worktree in its command line. Roughly half of one diagnostic matrix had to be
discarded and re-run.

Three things this costs, and each is a habit rather than a tool:

1. **Verify the sentinel around EVERY batch, not once at the start.** It is one
   HTTP request; the arms cost a minute each.
2. **Record the PID you started and re-check that the port's owner is still
   that PID.** `--strictPort` protects you at bind time and never again.
3. **Read a backgrounded launcher's exit status.** `exit 127` on a server you
   are actively measuring against is not a stale notification to skim past; it
   means everything after it is unattributed.

**The rule.** Port ownership is a claim with a lifetime, and the lifetime is
"until my process dies". Tie the claim to a PID you own, re-assert it as often
as you assert anything else, and treat any gap in the assertion as a gap in the
data.

### PAINT THE TERM. A ONE-LINE `gl_FragColor` OVERRIDE ANSWERS IN ONE BUILD WHAT A DOZEN ONE-FLAG ARMS CANNOT (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2305)

RN-2305 was chartered to remove "a hard texel-staircase shadow region" that
WORLD-AUDIT-R2 had already put through four one-flag negative controls. The lane
ran eight more -- `?shadows=0`, `?ao=0`, `?contact=0`, `?treeline=0`,
`?crownshade=0`, `?terrainart=0`, `?horizonocc=0`, `?cutoff=5|7` -- and every
one came back identical to the digit. Twelve controls, twelve nulls, and no
candidate left, because **a one-flag control can only ask about a term somebody
already thought to give a flag to.**

What settled it in four builds was replacing one line of the terrain fragment
shader with the term under suspicion and photographing it:

```glsl
gl_FragColor = vec4(lit, 1.0);
gl_FragColor = vec4(vec3(ndl), 1.0);   // then shadow, then sunT, then albedo
```

`ndl`: uniform white, no region. `shadow`: uniform white, no region. `sunT`:
uniform white, no region. `albedo`: **the region, with its staircase edge**. One
more paint, `vBiomeColor`, put three flat biome colours on the screen with the
same edge, and the "shadow" turned out to be the Forest ground palette meeting
the Hills ground palette across a one-cell barycentric blend on the coarse
terrain LOD.

**The rule.** A negative control tests a HYPOTHESIS; painting an intermediate
tests the PIPELINE. When the controls have all come back null the hypothesis
space is wrong, not the measurement, and the cheapest way out is to stop asking
"does removing X change the picture" and start asking "what does the picture
look like if it IS X". Cost: one line, one build, one frame, reverted before
commit -- with the bundle hash returning to HEAD's as the proof that it was.

---

### A LANE NAMED AFTER A MECHANISM WILL LOOK FOR THAT MECHANISM (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2305)

R1 called it "shadows stop at 300 m and the last cascade paints a texel
staircase". R2 called it "a hard texel-staircase shadow region ... its edge is
snapped to a texel grid, which is a shadow-map signature". Admin allocated a
lane called THE AERIAL SHADOW REGION, gave it the shadow files, and offered it
a fallback of "fade cascade shadows out with altitude". Three documents and a
work allocation, all naming the same mechanism, and the region is not a shadow:
it is two biome ground albedos meeting on a coarse vertex grid, and it survives
`?shadows=0` with the rig built at zero cascades and `renderer.shadowMap.enabled`
false, bit-identical.

The naming was not careless. "Hard-edged, regular, square-toothed, snapped to a
grid, present at three sun elevations" is a genuinely good description of a
cascade boundary. It is also a good description of any per-vertex quantity on a
quadtree mesh, and nobody wrote the second reading down because the first one
had a name and an owner already.

**The rule.** When a defect's name contains its diagnosis, the first arm of the
lane that inherits it is a control that would refute the name, and it is run
BEFORE any work that assumes the name is right. Here that arm was `?shadows=0`,
it cost one probe run, and it invalidated the lane's whole file partition: the
sun-invariance test (same pose, same site, sun azimuth moved by an hour and a
half) cost one more and would have done it alone.


---

### A DAYLIT FRAME CANNOT MEASURE A LIGHT SOURCE THE SUN IS LOUDER THAN, AND TWO AUDITS INFERRED WHERE ONE POSE COULD HAVE MEASURED (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2367, World Audit R3)

"Nothing emissive lights anything" has been a ranked gap since the first world
audit. Every frame it has ever rested on is a DAYLIT one: `smelterhero` and
`machine` at a pinned dot 0.448, and `basedusk`'s wall strip at dot 0.20. Those
frames support the sentence and they cannot support the measurement, because a
daylit frame cannot distinguish **an emissive that contributes nothing** from
**an emissive that contributes something forty decibels under the sun**, and
that distinction is the entire question a lane would be dispatched to answer. A
lane told "add bloom" would have shipped bloom; a lane told "the term is absent"
would have gone looking for an absent term. Neither brief was derivable.

The measurement cost **one manifest row derived by spread** from a shot that
already existed: `smelternight` is `smelterhero`'s pose, standoff, bearing and
all twelve rectangles to the digit at a sub-horizon sun, plus the one-flag
`?lamp=0` arm that removes the player's own light. It returns a number nobody
predicted: the whole frame reads **1.81** against an EMPTY MEADOW at the same
hour and the same flag at **2.03**. A running furnace makes the world measurably
darker than a bare field, because it occludes the sky and returns nothing. The
two emissive slabs glow (26.54 and 8.95) and every non-emissive rectangle in the
frame is at the ambient floor, including clean shell plate 0.3 m from the coals
at **2.72**.

**The rule.** When a claim is "X contributes nothing", the frame that tests it
must be one where X's contribution would be the DOMINANT signal, not one where
it competes with a source orders of magnitude larger. Ask what else is in the
frame and how much louder it is before believing a null; if the answer is "the
sun", the null is not evidence, it is the sun.

**And the corollary that made this cheap, which is worth as much as the
finding.** The instrument already existed. `smelterhero`'s manifest had long
since split the subject into emissive surfaces (`peep`, `strip`, and a `firebox`
rectangle chosen to EXCLUDE both emissive parts, with the reason written beside
it) and clean shell and brick that contain no fire (`plate`, `sunface`,
`hearthL`, `hearthR`). Those notes were written for a surface-materials pass and
they are exactly the split an emissive-light pass needs. **A manifest that says
why each rectangle is where it is can be re-aimed at a question it was not
written for; one that lists coordinates cannot.**

### A CONSTANT APPLIED AT EVERY VALUE OF A VARIABLE IT SHOULD DEPEND ON IS ONLY EVER SCORED IN THE MIDDLE OF THE RANGE (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2368, World Audit R3)

RN-2320 was chartered to stop the world reading as a sea from the air, and it
did: whole-frame `warm` at `flyovernoon` went -3.26 to +6.70 and three of four
aerial poses crossed or reached zero. Its lever was `aerosolTint`, changed from
a flat (0.32, 0.32, 0.32) to a flat (0.40, 0.31, 0.22) at the same mean. The
lane's pass condition was eight poses, four aerial and four ground, and every
one of them was measured and reported honestly.

**The tint is applied at every optical depth, and the pass condition only
contained one of them.** An aerial pose at 1,200 m looks through a few
kilometres of air. A 4.7 km ridge from a ridge-top looks through many more, and
a dawn anti-solar sky through more again. Measured one audit later, on the same
build the lane shipped: `vista.hzBand` warm **+22.46 -> +48.36** against a
`skyHz` at -12.14, so the ground and the sky now meet in a 60.5-count seam of
opposite hue where they used to meet in a 45.9-count one; and `dawnsun.skyUp`
crossed **-11.81 -> +7.19**, i.e. the one bearing in the whole sky that used to
go blue no longer does. The lane's own verifier found and published the second
of those as a disclosed side effect, which is the right thing to have done and
is why it was findable.

**The rule.** When a term is a CONSTANT with respect to a variable it physically
depends on, its pass condition must contain at least the two ENDS of that
variable's range, not the band the complaint came from. Otherwise the constant
is tuned where it was measured and is wrong everywhere else, and every reading
in the report is true. The tell is available before the measurement: ask what
the term multiplies, ask what that quantity ranges over in the shipped world,
and check whether the pose list spans it.

**Related and distinct** from "a metric that is flat in its own independent
variable is not measuring that variable": that one is about an instrument that
does not respond; this one is about a TERM that does not respond, to a variable
it should, and about a pose list that cannot see the difference.

---

### A REPEAT PROVES ITSELF WORLD-LOCKED BY CHANGING SCREEN PERIOD WITH RANGE, AND AN OFF-ARM THAT REMOVES THE DEFECT AND EVERYTHING ELSE IS A LOCATOR AND NOT A CONVICTION (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2369, World Audit R3)

> **FORWARD POINTER, added 2026-08-22 by RN-2452.** The instrument this entry
> describes (`latmeter.mjs`, committed by RN-2420) walks its lag window from
> `minLag = 4` and is therefore **structurally blind to a repeat whose period IS
> 4 px**, which is exactly what World Audit R4 found next. See "AN INSTRUMENT'S
> OWN FLOOR IS A CLASS OF DEFECT IT CAN NEVER REPORT" at the end of this file.
> Nothing below is wrong; its domain is narrower than it reads.

Two halves, both cheap, and the second is the one that stops an over-claim.

**Half one, the positive test.** This file already says an autocorrelation's
global maximum measures smoothness and that a repeat can only show as a LOCAL
maximum after the first local minimum. That establishes there IS a repeat. It
does not establish WHERE it lives, and a screen-space dither, a post-process
kernel and a world-space tile all produce a clean local maximum. **The test that
separates them is free and needs no second arm: measure the same repeat at two
screen heights on ONE frame.** A world-locked feature's screen period must grow
as the ground comes nearer; a screen-locked one cannot change at all. Measured
at `forestair`: 9.14 px at y540, 12.80 px at y660, and no peak in band at y820
where the tile has grown past the window. Take the negative control from the
same frame while you are there: a sky patch returns no local maximum at all
(best after its first minimum is -0.224), which proves the instrument can say
"no repeat" on a real image rather than only on a synthetic.

**Half two, and it is the discipline half.** Seven one-flag art isolators
(`?canopy=0`, `?treeline=0`, `?splat=0`, `?splatfar=0`, `?groundtexamp=0`,
`?terrainart=0`, `?horizon=0`) left the repeat untouched to two decimal places.
`?split=2.8`, which coarsens the terrain mesh, removed it completely: patch std
6.21 -> 3.19, no local maximum out to lag 176. That is very tempting to write
down as "it is the mesh". **It is not a conviction, because the same arm removed
every other trace of ground material at that range as well**: the frame's right
half is a featureless plane. An arm that deletes the defect AND its whole
neighbourhood locates the defect in that neighbourhood and says nothing about
which member of it is responsible. It is the "an arm that deletes a whole
subsystem measures the subsystem" entry one level finer: here the subsystem is
not a named feature, it is everything downstream of one shared input.

**The rule.** Report such an arm as a LOCATOR: "it lives inside this family" is
a real result and is worth publishing. Do not upgrade it to a named cause. And
when every flag in the space has come back null, the next step is RN-2305's:
paint the intermediate, do not add another flag. This audit published the
finding undiagnosed with all seven nulls, both world-lock controls and the
locator, and named the painted intermediate as the receiving lane's first
deliverable.

---

### A GUARD THAT REFUSES A MALFORMED INSTRUMENT SETUP LOUDLY IN 0.4 SECONDS IS THE CHEAPEST ENTRY IN THIS FILE (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2370, World Audit R3)

Recorded as a POSITIVE, because this catalogue is almost entirely a list of
things that failed quietly and it is worth naming the shape that does not.

This audit's first control matrix built its arms by appending flags to the URL:
`--url=http://127.0.0.1:5865/?aerosol=0`. `run.mjs` refuses that outright:

    smoke: --url must not carry a query string. '?aerosol=0' would be silently
    discarded, because the runner rebuilds the query from its own flags. Pass
    the flags instead: --url=http://127.0.0.1:5865/ plus e.g. --sandbox=1 ...

Sixteen arms exited 2 in 0.4 s each. **Without that guard all sixteen would have
booted a shipped build, run to completion, and returned sixteen plausible
byte-identical nulls**, which this file already records as the most dangerous
result a control can produce ("a byte-identical null across every rectangle is a
stronger signal of an inert instrument than of an inert term"). The audit would
then have concluded that the aerosol does not touch the far ridge, that the
carpet does not flatten the mid field and that the headlamp is not what lights
the night, and every one of those conclusions is the opposite of what the armed
arms say.

**The rule, for anyone writing a harness rather than using one.** Where an
interface has a way of being used that is silently ignored, refuse it at the
door with a message that names the correct form. It is one branch, it fires in
under a second, and its whole value is the family of wrong answers it never lets
anybody publish. **The guard's payoff is invisible in every run where it does
not fire, which is why it has to be argued for once, in writing, here.**

---

### AN INSTRUMENT'S OWN FLOOR IS A CLASS OF DEFECT IT CAN NEVER REPORT, AND THE FIX IS A SECOND INSTRUMENT RATHER THAN A LOWERED FLOOR (found 2026-08-22 by RN-2452, World Audit R4)

`latmeter.mjs` exists because of this file's own entry that an autocorrelation's
global maximum measures smoothness and a repeat can only show as a LOCAL maximum
after the first local minimum. It walks its lag window from `minLag = 4`, which
is correct for the defect it was built for: R3's aerial lattice had a period of
9 to 13 px.

**R4's lattice has a period of exactly 4 px, and `latmeter` reports "no local
maximum" on a frame where the grid is unmissable by eye at 1x.** Not a small
reading. Nothing. The instrument that the project had just spent a lane
sharpening was structurally incapable of seeing the successor to the defect it
was sharpened on, and it said so in the language of a clean result.

**The tempting fix is to lower the floor and it is wrong.** `minLag` is not a
tuning constant, it is the boundary between two different measurements: below it
the autocorrelation is reporting blur, above it a repeat. Lower it and every
latmeter number this project has published silently changes meaning, including
the ones a landed lane's done-when is written against.

**What was done instead**, and it is the general recommendation: leave the
instrument alone and write a second one that asks the question the new defect
actually poses. `rn2450bayer.mjs` bins every pixel by `(x mod p, y mod p)` --
the exact index a `mod(gl_FragCoord.xy, 4.0)` ordered dither uses -- and reports
the spread over the p*p phase means, with the patch std beside it so that a
"fix" that removes the pattern by removing the material shows up as one.

**And it ships with a free negative control that runs on the same pixels.**
`--p=5`. A genuine 4-px dither has nothing at period 5, so a patch that reports a
large spread at both is reporting image structure rather than a dither. That
control cost one flag and it is what makes the p=4 reading a measurement instead
of an assertion: at `vistadawn` the shipped frame reads phaseStd 1.791 at p=4 and
1.198 at p=5, and `?contact=0` takes p=4 to **0.602** while p=5 goes UP to 1.403.

**The rule.** Every instrument has a domain, and its boundary is usually a
constant somebody chose for the first defect it met. When a new defect lands
outside that boundary the instrument does not error, it returns the shape of a
clean result. **Before believing a null from a mature instrument, check that the
thing you are looking for is inside its domain at all** -- for a period measure
that means the period, for a rectangle it means the pixels the term can reach,
for a fraction it means the denominator. And when it is not, prefer a second
instrument with its own control over a widened first one, because the first one's
numbers are load-bearing elsewhere.

---

### A LANE'S DELTAS SURVIVE A LATER MERGE AND ITS ABSOLUTE LEVELS DO NOT (found 2026-08-22 by RN-2455, World Audit R4)

Five lanes were dispatched off one audit and landed in four separate merges. The
fourth of them, M2, published a before/after table on its own base
(`4a8ac1bf`, which carried two of its siblings and not the third).

Re-measured on merged `main` through M2's own one-flag isolator, its three
headline rectangles read:

| rectangle | M2 published | measured on merged main |
|---|---|---|
| `vista.hzBand` iqr | 2.21 -> 3.07 (+0.86) | 2.61 -> 3.28 (**+0.67**) |
| `vista.mid` iqr | 14.36 -> 17.08 (+2.72) | 11.33 -> 13.96 (**+2.63**) |
| `vista.nearG` iqr | 19.22 -> 17.14 (-2.08) | 26.78 -> 25.00 (**-1.78**) |

**Every DELTA reproduces -- same sign, within 0.3 counts -- and not one LEVEL
does**, by up to 7.9. Nothing is wrong with either measurement. The lane measured
its own change correctly against the tree it built on; the audit measured the
shipped world correctly against the tree that exists.

Two consequences, and the second is the one that costs.

- **A lane's own published levels expire at its merge.** They are a snapshot of a
  tree that stopped existing. A later lane briefed against them will chase a
  discrepancy that is arithmetic.
- **A DISCLOSED REGRESSION IS A LEVEL, so its published size is wrong the moment
  the merge lands.** M2 disclosed an 11 per cent `vista.nearG` cost in good faith
  and routed it as an owed item. On merged main it is **6.6 per cent**. A queue
  ranked on the 11 would over-weight it, and a verifier checking the 11 would
  find it "does not reproduce" and be right and be misled.

**The rule.** Publish the DELTA as the claim and the level as context, and say
which base the level was read on in the same sentence. When a lane's figure is
going to be carried forward as an owed item, the receiving audit re-measures it
on merged main rather than transcribing it -- and where the two differ, that is
composition, not a defect, and the audit says so rather than filing a
discrepancy.

### A DOCSTRING THAT NAMES A CAUSE OUTLIVES THE CAUSE, AND FOUR AUDITS WILL CHASE IT (found 2026-08-22 by RN-2456, World Audit R4)

This file already says a sentence in a comment is not an invariant. **This is its
sharper sibling: a comment that names a SUSPECT is a suspect with an owner, and
it keeps its authority after the code it describes has gone.**

A canonical shot has photographed the wrong thing in six consecutive audits. Its
manifest row carries a long, careful, honest diagnosis naming a leading suspect:
two authorities on one object's orientation, with two different roll conventions,
one applied at install and one per tick. Three audits and one dispatched lane
inherited that suspect. It is false, and it has been false since a commit that
predates the first of them: there is one writer, the install-time call fires the
same watcher the per-tick path does, and the commit that removed the second
authority says so in as many words two dozen lines below.

**What kept the dead suspect alive was two docstrings that were never updated
when the code changed.** One is a file header describing the pre-fix design; the
other still states, as present tense, the exact claim the fix removed. Both read
as authoritative because both sit in the files a reader would check.

**And the evidence FOR the suspect did not survive reading either.** The row's
strongest sentence is "same camera, same eye, same direction, two different
scenes". The camera certificate it rests on is built, by the probe's own comment
twenty lines away, BEFORE the capture call, in a frame that a second comment says
cannot see the floating origin. Nobody checked whether the certificate was of the
photographed frame, because the certificate agreed with the suspect.

**Three rules.**

- **When a fix removes a mechanism, grep for the mechanism's NAME and fix the
  prose in the same commit.** A removed cause with a surviving description is
  worse than an undocumented one, because the description is what the next reader
  will reason from.
- **A long, well-written, honest diagnosis is not more likely to be current than
  a short one.** This one was exemplary in every respect except being true, and
  its quality is exactly why four rounds deferred to it.
- **Before inheriting a named suspect, run the one arm that would refute it.**
  That is this file's "a lane named after a mechanism will look for that
  mechanism", applied to a suspect that lives in a comment rather than in a lane's
  title. Here the refutation was a grep for the second call site and it cost
  minutes.

### EVERY RECTANGLE THAT MEASURED "THE FAR GROUND" WAS AT ONE SITE, AND THE SITE THE PLAYER SPAWNS IN WAS NEVER MEASURED (found 2026-08-22 by RN-2453, World Audit R4)

This file already records that a shot set can be structurally blind to its own
subject, and that adding shots is cheaper than arguing. **This is that entry one
level finer, and the finer level is the one that survived it: the shot set had
the poses. It was the RECTANGLES that were all in one place.**

"The far ground has no material past about 75 m" has been a ranked gap for four
audits. Three lanes worked on it and two audits scored it. Every number any of
them used -- `vista.hzBand`, `vista.mid`, `vistanoon.mid`, `flyovernoon.under` --
frames the same mountain massif at the same ridge-top site. The third audit
scored the gap HALF CLOSED on the strength of those rectangles quadrupling.

The plains biome, which is where the game starts and where four of the canonical
poses stand, has exactly one committed rectangle past 100 m in the entire
project. It reads iqr **4.06** today against **3.99** one audit ago and it has
never moved. By eye those four frames put a flat, untextured plane past about 130
metres, meeting the sky at a razor-straight line. The gap was not half closed; it
was closed at a mountain and never looked at where the player stands.

**And the two sites do not even have the same CAUSE.** At the vista site the
audit's own control concluded "the lever at that range is the air, not the
ground": the ridge and the airlight sat within two counts of each other. At the
plains site the same control (`?aerosol=0`) buys **0.79 counts** on a 4-count
rectangle, so there is nothing out there for the air to be hiding and the lever
is the ground. A single lane briefed from the vista-site conclusion would have
tuned an atmosphere constant and closed nothing.

**Two rules.**

- **When a gap is scored on a set of rectangles, list the SITES those rectangles
  live at before believing the score generalises.** A gap that is a property of
  the world is measured in more than one biome; a gap measured in one is a
  statement about that biome until someone checks.
- **A pose is not coverage.** The plains poses existed the whole time and were
  photographed in every audit. What was missing was a rectangle, which is an
  afternoon, and its absence let a BLOCKING surface gap read as half closed for
  two rounds.

### A RECTANGLE CAN BE ON THE WRONG SIDE OF THE HORIZON, AND THREE AUDITS WILL READ ITS STILLNESS AS A PROPERTY OF THE GROUND (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2475, lane N1)

The entry above says the far-ground rectangles were all at one SITE. This is the
same defect one level finer and it is worse, because the fix for the entry above
was "add a rectangle at the other site" and the rectangle at the other site was
already there and was pointing at the sky.

`meadow.hzBand` was quoted in three consecutive audits as the evidence for "the
plains far ground is a flat painted plane": iqr **4.06**, then 3.99, then 4.06,
unmoved. **It contains no terrain.** Paint every terrain fragment magenta and it
returns rgb 214.11 / 207.55 / 188.64 against a shipped 214.08 / 207.56 / 188.60,
identical to a hundredth of a count, while `vista.hzBand` under the same paint on
the same build comes back fully painted. The rectangle sits at frame rows 270 to
306; a row profile puts that pose's horizon at rows **317 to 325**. Its 4.06 is
the haze band's own per-row iqr, which reads 3.93 to 4.20 on every row above the
horizon.

Two things follow and both were published as findings before this was noticed.
**"It has not moved in three audits" was read as a fact about the terrain** when
no terrain term can move it. And **`?aerosol=0` at that rectangle buys 0.79
counts** was read as "the lever is the ground and not the air", i.e. an argument
about the ground, from an arm run entirely on sky. (That conclusion happened to
survive: on a rectangle that can see the subject the same arm moves it by 0.01
counts. It survived by luck, not by method.)

**The rule.** A rectangle whose name asserts a subject is a claim, and the cheap
way to check it is a one-line paint that colours the subject and nothing else:
if the rectangle does not move, it is not looking at what it is named for. Run it
BEFORE a number from that rectangle is quoted in a conclusion, and certainly
before it is quoted three times. The corollary is the useful half: **a control
that reads as a null is only evidence if the rectangle it was read on contains
the term's subject.**

### THE HARNESS'S RANGE MAP AND THE SHADER'S OWN FOOTPRINT DISAGREE BY AN ORDER OF MAGNITUDE, AND A FIX SIZED AGAINST THE WRONG ONE IS INERT (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2479, lane N1)

`artframe.js`'s `rangeRects` publishes `rangeM` and `footM` per rectangle by
inverting a FLAT PLANE at the observer's eye height, pitch and fov. At
`midfield` it reports a pixel footprint of 0.257 m at 18 m, 0.957 at 35, 2.79 at
60, 11.1 at 120, **48.6 at 250** and 292 at 600 -- growing as the square of the
range, which is correct arithmetic for a plane.

A whole fix was designed against those numbers: two coarser noise octaves, sized
so their Nyquist fades covered the band where every existing octave had retired
at a 48-to-292 m footprint. It was built, wired to its own uniform and query
flag, typechecked, shipped to a preview and measured. **At twenty times its
shipped amplitude it moved the rectangle by 0.00 counts.**

The shader's `footM` is `max(length(dFdx(vWorld)), length(dFdy(vWorld)))`.
Painted as a `step()` ladder at the material's own gate boundaries (1.8 / 8.0 /
20.0 / 53.3 / 213.0 m), exactly one step passes at that rectangle: the shader
sees **between 1.8 and 8.0 m** where the manifest says 48.6. The ground at that
site is not a plane -- it swells, so the visible horizon is a crest a few hundred
metres out rather than the geometric one, and the incidence is nothing like
grazing. Both effects shrink the footprint and they compound.

**Two rules.** A harness range map is a reproducible PLACEMENT, not a survey, and
it says so in its own header; **do not size a shader gate against it.** And when
a term must fire inside a band, **paint the band's own value of the quantity the
gate reads** before spending a build on the term -- one `step()` ladder would have
killed this design in an afternoon instead of after it was written.

### PAINT A DIAGNOSTIC INTO THE BOTTOM OF THE TONE CURVE, NOT THE TOP (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2479, lane N1)

The painted-intermediate method writes a term's value into `lit` and reads it
back off the frame. It is read through the shipped grade, and this project's
grade is an ACES fit at exposure 1.2 with contrast 1.45, which is brutally
compressive above about 0.3: on one build a painted **0.25 photographs at 177.55,
0.5 at about 207 and 1.0 at 215.76**, so the whole upper half of a term's range
arrives as nine counts and a five-level ladder becomes unreadable.

Two arms in one lane were read wrong that way and had to be re-run at one fifth
scale. **Scale a painted scalar so its full range lands under about 0.25, and
prefer a `step()` ladder to a continuous value: a step is exact, a level is a
question about the grade.** Zero is the one value that survives the curve
unambiguously, which is why "is this gate exactly zero" is the strongest question
a paint can answer and should be the first one asked.
### AN ARM TABLE'S HEADER NAMES ONE BUILD, AND A ROW TAKEN MID-SEARCH INTERPOLATES TO A PLAUSIBLE NUMBER THAT REPRODUCES NOWHERE (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2495, verified by a fresh-context verifier)

**The shape.** A diagnosis lane builds a one-flag-apart attribution table:
header says "baseline, one page param apart, fresh process each", rows say
`?termA=0`, `?termB=0`, and so on. The lane then starts its constant search,
edits the constant, rebuilds, and **keeps adding rows to the same table**. Every
new row is now taken against a candidate build, not against the baseline the
header names.

**Why nothing catches it.** Each individual capture is impeccable. The server is
sentinel-verified, the process is fresh, the repeat is bit-identical, the flag
is registered, the arm is genuinely one page param from the build it ran on.
Every rail this project has passes. The defect is not in any capture; it is in
the JOIN between captures that the table's header silently asserts.

**Why it is worse than a wrong number.** A mid-search row does not land
somewhere absurd, which is what `AN IMPLAUSIBLE MAGNITUDE IS AN INSTRUMENT BUG`
would catch. It lands on the INTERPOLATION between the baseline arm and the
shipped arm, so it has the right sign, the right order of magnitude, and it
supports whatever conclusion the lane was drafting when it took the row. RN-2495
published `?crownshadecard=0` at 6.59 and `?crownshadefar=0` at 12.85 against a
baseline of 3.92; the true baseline readings are **4.80** and **9.31**, and
inverting the interpolation puts the published pair at an effective canopy
saturation of about 0.96 and 0.93, which were literally two of the lane's own
candidate constants. **The corrected costs reorder the table**: the card half
falls from 2.67 to 0.88 and the far paint from 8.93 to 5.39, which flips the
lane's own lever from third-largest term to second and re-aims the routed
follow-up at a different half of a different file.

**The rule.** *An arm table's header names one build, and every row in it must
come from that build in one session.* Not "from a build with that constant" and
not "from an equivalent arm": one session, one server, one `dist`. When the
constant moves, the WHOLE table is stale, including the rows that have nothing
to do with the constant, because the reader cannot tell which is which.

**The cheap enforcement, and it costs one flag.** Give the constant a page-param
override whose default is the shipped row (RN-2495's `?canopysat=`). The
baseline then remains reachable from the FINAL build as a one-flag arm, so the
whole table can be re-taken in one command at the end of the lane, and no row
ever has to be inherited from the search. Re-taking eight arms cost eight
minutes; the interpolated pair survived into three published documents.

**The tell, for a reviewer.** A row in an arm table whose value sits strictly
between the baseline and the shipped arm, on a term that should be independent
of the shipped change, is that row. Ask when it was captured, not whether it
reproduces on the build in front of you.

### A SHOT THAT TURNS THE SUBJECT OFF BY DECLARATION WILL BE REASONED FROM ANYWAY, AND THE DECLARATION IS SIX HUNDRED LINES ABOVE THE NUMBER (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2510, lane N4)

`artframe.js`'s `midfield` row carries `props: false`. It is deliberate, its own
manifest note explains why, and RN-2478's rectangle note repeats it. It still
produced two lanes of wrong reasoning: N1's eye verdict at 2.30.9 concluded "a
real plain carries objects standing on it and ours carries nothing", Admin
turned that into a lane charter, and both readings were taken on a pose from
which **every object had been removed by declaration**. At the sibling pose that
keeps them, `?props=0` moves the same-named rectangle by **3.88 counts of iqr
and 19.52 of luma**: the objects are there, they are dark, and they add almost
no structure -- a completely different defect from "nothing is there", requiring
a completely different lane.

**This is the site-blindness entry one level in: not the wrong SITE and not the
wrong SIDE OF THE HORIZON, but the wrong SCENE at the right site.** The two
earlier entries are about where a rectangle sits; this one is about what the
manifest deleted before the shutter opened.

**The rule. A judgement about what a frame CONTAINS may only be read on a pose
that contains it.** Before quoting any rectangle as evidence for a claim about
objects, vegetation, structures or shadows, read the pose's own manifest row for
a `props`, `canopy`, `gameplay` or `station` field that switches that layer off,
and say in the report which pose the number came from and what that pose
declares. A shot set with deliberate ablation poses in it is a good shot set;
the failure is quoting one without saying so.

### A TERM SPLICED INTO A `#ifndef OF_SCALED` REGION IS ABSENT FROM THE FAR GROUND, AND ITS SWEEP LOOKS LIKE A WEAK TERM RATHER THAN A MISSING ONE (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2514, lane N4)

`TerrainFragAlbedo.glsl.ts` compiles twice, one `#define` apart, and lines 118
to 340 -- the whole splat branch, which is where every other albedo cover term
lives -- are one `#ifndef OF_SCALED` block. A new far-field term written beside
its natural neighbour therefore reached the near program only. Its amplitude
sweep moved the rectangle a little, monotonically, in a plausible direction, and
read for an afternoon as a term that was simply too weak.

**The isolator that settled it in one build was a magenta paint INSIDE the
term's own branch, not a sweep of its amplitude.** With the term where it was,
the whole band under the horizon came back unpainted while the ground nearer
than it went magenta; moved out of the region, the band from the ring to the
horizon painted. `MASSIF_FADE_M`'s own docstring already records the same thing
from the other side ("the massif block and its normal half are compiled into
BOTH programs, so there is no side of the handover where the term is missing"),
and it is why RN-2475's plains gain reached that band while a term written
thirty lines away could not.

**The rule. For any term whose subject is past the near program's reach, paint
the term's own branch before sweeping its amplitude.** A sweep answers "how
strong is it here"; a paint answers "is it here at all", and only the second
question has a null answer that looks like a small number.

### AN AMPLITUDE CANNOT SPLIT `col * T + Lin`, SO A HAZE FLAG PRICES BOTH HALVES AND ATTRIBUTES NEITHER (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2540, lane N7)

Aerial perspective, fog, any veil: the shipped pixel is `surface * T + Lin`, a
MULTIPLY and an ADD in one term. The project's controls for it were amplitudes
(`?prophaze=`, and for a whole year the terrain had none at all), and an
amplitude moves both halves together. `?prophaze=0` at the crowns rectangle
moves blue by 28.48 counts, and that single number is the extinction the surface
stops losing PLUS the in-scatter it stops gaining, in unknown proportion. Four
audits and two lanes reasoned about a blue cast from numbers of exactly that
shape.

**THE FIX IS A PAINT ARM, AND IT COSTS ONE `mix`.** Zero the SOURCE RADIANCE
before the term and leave the term itself untouched:

```glsl
vec3 src = mix(lit, vec3(0.0), uApPaint);   // 0 is the shipped frame, exactly
vec3 apLit = src * apTrans + apIn;
apLit = ofAtmoAerial(apLit, ...);
lit = mix(src, apLit, uApAmp);              // 1 is the shipped frame, exactly
```

The fragment then renders `Lin` ALONE, on the real geometry, at the real range,
through the real phase function, with no model standing in for any of it. Two
arms and one subtraction split the term. Both defaults are algebraic identities,
so the pair is still one uniform apart on one program.

**AND THE COMPLEMENTARY PAIR GIVES A CLOSURE CHECK NOTHING ELSE DOES.** Painting
surface A black leaves `(1-f) x B` and painting B black leaves `f x A`, so the
two arms must sum to the shipped rectangle. At RN-2540's own site they summed to
within 0.65 counts of 80.67 on every channel, which is what earns the right to
quote a 91.9-per-cent attribution off them. A decomposition with no closure
check is a division nobody has audited.

**A COROLLARY WORTH THE LINE.** The same arms priced the two ends of the term
separately and found the ATTRIBUTION inverted the intuition: the surface's own
albedo was 0.03 per cent of the pixel and the additive floor was 91.9 per cent,
so the constant three lanes had been tuning could not have moved the picture at
any value. An amplitude arm would have shown a large delta and been read as
"the term matters", which is true and useless.

### `vite preview` ANSWERS 200 FOR EVERY MISSING PATH, SO A SENTINEL CHECKED ON STATUS CODE IS NOT A SENTINEL (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2540's fresh-context verifier)

The sentinel rule in this file is "write a unique token into your own `dist`,
fetch it back over the wire, and do not trust the server until it comes back".
The trap is in how it gets checked. **`vite preview` serves a single-page app,
so an unknown path is not a 404: it falls back to `index.html` and returns
HTTP 200 with a body.** A check written as "did the request succeed" therefore
passes against:

- a server started from a DIFFERENT worktree's `dist` (the token file is absent
  there, the SPA fallback answers 200, the check is green, and every number
  after it describes another lane's build);
- a foreign process that grabbed the port first (the verifier of RN-2495 hit
  exactly this: a stranger's PID on 5751 answering with an SPA fallback);
- a build where `dist` was never written at all.

**THE TOKEN'S CONTENT IS THE CHECK, NOT THE STATUS CODE.** Compare the bytes
that come back against the bytes just written, and make the token unique per
build rather than per lane so a stale `dist` from your own earlier build fails
too. RN-2540 used a distinct token on each of its five builds
(`RN2540-<letter>-<epoch ms>`) precisely so a reused `dist` could not pass, and
the pre-lane control build's token differed from the lane build's, which is what
makes its bit-identity pair mean anything.

A one-line smell test for any existing harness: request a path that certainly
does not exist. If it answers 200, every status-code check pointed at that
server has been vacuous for as long as it has existed.
---

### A ROUTED MECHANISM IS STILL A HYPOTHESIS, AND THE NUMBER REPRODUCING IS NOT THE MECHANISM REPRODUCING (found 2026-08-21 by WG-278, lane `lane/wg-ship`)

WG-244 measured a real coupling and routed it to rendering in one sentence:
"`midfield.r250` moves 43.83 -> 35.20, because the swell moves `vRelief`, which
is the input to `MASSIF_BAND`, so a height change at a plain silently retunes
RN-2480's own gain." It was recorded in a controller file, quoted in a banner,
carried into an allocation table, and turned into an instruction on the next
lane's brief: re-derive the gain.

**The number is exact and reproduces to the digit. The mechanism does not
exist.** `hzMsfBand` is `smoothstep(MASSIF_BAND[0], MASSIF_BAND[1], vRelief /
uMaxRelief)` and the gate's start is 0.10 of a 6,000 m normaliser, i.e. **600 m
of relief**. The probe's own `world.surfaceHeightM` at that site reads
**331.83 m before and 355.86 m after**. Both are below the gate by 245 m, so
`hzMsfBand` is exactly zero on both sides and the multiplier is 1.5x in both
arms. Corroborated one flag apart: `?horizonmassif=0` moves the rectangle by
**0.00 counts in BOTH arms**, so the term on the far side of the complement is
not drawing there at all. What actually moved the rectangle was the ground: the
change's finest octave is 1 km, which puts real height variation into the 250 m
ring the rectangle measures.

Three things make this shape expensive rather than merely wrong.

1. **The routing carried the mechanism, not the measurement.** A number with a
   cause attached reads as explained, and a downstream lane spends its budget on
   the cause. This one arrived as "re-derive the gain", which is an afternoon of
   arm ladders answering a question nothing had asked.
2. **The cause was checkable from data the reporting lane already had.**
   `surfaceHeightM` is in every probe report and `MASSIF_BAND` is a two-element
   export. The arithmetic is one division and one comparison. Nobody did it,
   because the mechanism was plausible and the number was right.
3. **Being right about the number is what made it survive review.** Three
   readers checked 43.83 -> 35.20, found it, and passed the sentence on. A wrong
   number gets caught; a right number with a wrong reason attached gets
   corroborated.

**The rule. When routing a cross-domain item, publish the MEASUREMENT as the
claim and the mechanism as a hypothesis with the check that would settle it, or
do the check.** "X moved from A to B" is a fact. "X moved because Y" is a second
finding and it needs its own evidence, especially when the fact is solid enough
that nobody will re-examine the sentence attached to it. The receiving lane's
first duty is to test the mechanism before spending anything on it, and to say
so out loud when it does not survive, because a refuted cause left standing in
three documents will be re-routed by the next audit.

---

### A DELTA CAN GROW ACROSS A MERGE, NOT ONLY SHRINK, WHEN A SIBLING LANE GIVES IT SOMETHING TO STAND ON (found 2026-08-21 by WG-277, lane `lane/wg-ship`)

The entry above about deltas and levels ("A LANE'S DELTAS SURVIVE A LATER MERGE
AND ITS ABSOLUTE LEVELS DO NOT") says deltas reproduce within a fraction of a
count while levels drift. That held in the case it was written from, where the
composing changes were independent. **It does not hold when two merged changes
are multiplicative, and the failure is much larger than the drift it replaces.**

A height-field lane measured `meadow.hzBand` iqr moving **4.06 to 12.29** on its
own base. Shipped onto merged `main`, the same change, one flag apart on one
binary, reads **4.21 to 155.83**. The LEVEL drifted by 0.15, exactly as the
earlier entry predicts. The DELTA went from 3.03x to 37.0x.

Neither measurement is wrong. The change lifts ground into a rectangle that was
pure sky. On the original base the risen ground was bare, and its tone sat close
to the haze it displaced. Between the two measurements a sibling lane added
mid-distance tree stands, which are dark, so the same risen ground now arrives
carrying a silhouette and the rectangle goes bimodal (p05 36.72, p50 119.63,
p95 211.11 against a flat 201.72 of haze on the off arm). **One change supplies
the geometry and the other supplies the contrast, and neither produces the
reading alone.** Proved rather than argued: running the shipped arm with the
sibling's own kill switch reproduces **12.29 exactly**.

**The rule. Before quoting a predecessor's delta, ask whether anything merged
since could be a MULTIPLIER on it rather than an addend.** Where the answer is
yes, the predecessor's figure is not stale by a fraction, it is a different
measurement, and the honest re-take is a one-flag arm against the sibling's own
switch so the two contributions are separated instead of summed. A delta quoted
across a merge needs its co-factors named, the same way a level needs its base
named.

### THE `+dirty` BUILD STAMP BREAKS A DIST-HASH IDENTITY TEST FOR A LANE THAT CHANGED NO RENDERING CODE (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2550, lane N8)

Hashing the whole `dist` tree is the cheapest and strongest way for a
no-pixel-change lane to prove itself: a byte-identical bundle cannot render a
different pixel, and it costs one command instead of a from-scratch pre-lane
build and a rect-by-rect table.

It reports a false positive. `vite.config.ts` defines `__OF_BUILD__` (BT-27)
from `git rev-parse --short HEAD` plus a **`+dirty`** suffix whenever
`git diff --name-only HEAD -- web core` is non-empty. So an UNCOMMITTED lane
that edits any tracked file under `web/` -- a probe, a tool script, anything at
all outside `src/` -- flips the stamp from `<sha>` to `<sha>+dirty`, and that
string is compiled into the main entry chunk. Three files then differ: the entry
chunk, its source map, and `index.html`, which names the chunk by its content
hash. The lane looks like it moved the bundle. It did not.

**The fix is one environment variable, and it should be the default way this
test is run:** build both sides with `OF_BUILD_STAMP` forced to the same value.
The config already honours it, for exactly this class of reason. On the lane
that found this, the forced build came back byte-identical across all 170 files
against a `63c66a68...`-versus-`5f0a7649...` mismatch without it.

Two smaller lessons came with it. **Committing first also hides the problem
rather than solving it**, because the stamp then carries the lane's own sha and
still differs. And when the per-file diff was first taken, one snapshot was
listed from the repo root and the other from `web/`, so the path prefixes
differed and `diff` reported **all 170 files as changed** -- an instrument bug
inside the instrument built to chase an instrument bug. Normalise the paths
before believing a whole-tree diff.

### AVERAGING BEFORE DECODING IS NOT DECODING BEFORE AVERAGING, AND THE ERROR DOES NOT CANCEL IN A RATIO (found 2026-08-21 by RN-2550, lane N8)

Any time an 8-bit patch mean is linearized, there are two orders available and
they give different numbers. Decoding the patch MEAN is not the mean of the
patch's DECODED pixels: the sRGB inverse EOTF is convex, so by Jensen the
per-pixel answer is always the larger, by a term that grows with the patch's own
**variance**.

The trap is the reflex that says it cancels in a ratio. It cancels only if both
patches have the same variance, and the interesting pair almost never does. The
case that found it: a wood patch against the same rectangle with the vegetation
removed, where `box` iqr is **34.70 on the wood against 27.92 on the clearing**.
Measured on the same pixels at `forestairnoon`, the four defensible routes to
"the ratio" give **0.9840** (raw 8-bit), **0.9664** (decode the luma scalar),
**0.9680** (average the channels, then decode) and **0.9894** (decode per pixel,
then average). Averaging first costs up to **0.0285** across the four poses and
**always flatters the higher-variance patch**.

Two rules fall out.

**Decode per pixel, then average.** The mean radiance of a patch is the mean of
its pixels' radiances; anything else is a number with no physical referent.

**Decode per channel, never the luma scalar.** Luminance is a linear functional
of LINEAR radiance, so the EOTF goes on R, G and B and the weights go on the
decoded values. Decoding an already-mixed 8-bit luma applies a channel transfer
function to a quantity that is not a channel. That error is smaller here (under
**0.0016**) but it is wrong in principle and it is free to avoid.

The reason this belongs in the catalogue rather than in one lane's record: the
spread across those four routes was **0.0230** at the pose in question, which in
that pose's own terms was **larger than the entire margin the guard being
replaced had lived on**. A threshold whose decode order is unstated is a
threshold a later lane can satisfy by choosing how to average, without ever
knowing it made a choice.
